summary: Explains the Internet calendaring and scheduling standards (iCalendar, iTIP, iMIP) and how they relate. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3283 explains how several standards support sharing calendar information and scheduling meetings. It distinguishes the format for calendar data from the messages used to arrange events and the ways those messages can be sent.

questions: how do icalendar itip and imip relate
how are calendar invitations sent by email
subtitle: How the Internet calendaring standards fit together and where they leave gaps.

tldr.problem: People and organizations need to exchange calendar data and schedule with users of different systems. This RFC explains the roles of the calendaring standards and the problems they do not address.
tldr.mechanism: iCalendar represents calendar information, iTIP defines scheduling messages, and iMIP carries iTIP through email. CAP was a work in progress for real-time calendar-store access when this RFC was written.
tldr.outcome: The Informational guide gives implementers context and examples. It also identifies gaps such as administration, finding a person's correct calendar address, and real-time change notifications.

today: RFC 3283 is an Informational guide published in June 2002. It describes CAP as work in progress and identifies issues left open by the protocols it discusses.

sections.title: The Calendaring Standards
sections.content:
iCalendar defines the format for calendar objects such as events, to-dos and alarms. iTIP uses that format for scheduling actions, including invitations, replies, changes and requests for free/busy information. iTIP does not depend on one transport.

iMIP binds iTIP to email. At the time of this RFC, Calendar Access Protocol (CAP) was work in progress; it described real-time access to a calendar store, including search and calendar-management operations. The RFC is a guide to the relationships among these specifications, not a specification of their protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: iCalendar is the format for calendar information, and iTIP is the set of messages used to schedule events. iMIP carries those messages by email, while CAP was a proposal for direct access to a calendar service.

sections.title: What Calendar Users Need
sections.content:
The RFC describes six situations: one person managing a calendar, a person using multiple devices, colleagues sharing schedules, students booking appointments, a theater publishing its schedule, and a club arranging events across services. Some situations can use proprietary systems, but the guide says cross-vendor exchange needs common protocols and a common data format.

For a single user who does not communicate with other systems, no calendaring protocol is required, though iCalendar may be useful as a storage or exchange format. For users on separate systems, iTIP over email through iMIP is one option; a calendar service accessed with CAP was another option described in the document.
sections.plainLanguage: One person's calendar can be private, but sharing across different systems requires shared rules. The RFC shows how common tasks can work across calendar programs and devices.

sections.title: Practical Limits and Open Issues
sections.content:
Implementers need to account for time zones, large calendar components, and complex recurrence rules. A direct network protocol may require firewall changes. Email can carry scheduling messages through existing mail systems, but delivery delay may be unbounded.

The described protocols do not identify one person's correct calendar among several addresses and stores, define user or calendar administration, or provide real-time notification of new or changed items. Clients may need to poll a store for changes. These are limitations noted by the RFC, not features supplied by its guide.
sections.plainLanguage: Calendar systems must handle time zones, repeating events, and messages of different sizes. The protocols described here do not choose the right calendar for a person or automatically notify clients when stored data changes.

sections.title: Access and Message Security
sections.content:
A calendar service needs access rules that control which information a requester may read or change. The RFC says access control must be paired with authentication so the service can identify requesters before releasing information. CAP uses the Simple Authentication and Security Layer (SASL) in the guide's description.

Email scheduling messages may lack authentication, which makes sender spoofing and calendar spam possible. The RFC suggests that implementers consider requiring authentication by default and consider signing and encryption. Systems that process requests automatically also need to consider denial-of-service attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: Calendar details can be private, so a service needs to check who is requesting them and what that person may see. Email invitations can be forged, so systems should consider ways to verify and protect those messages.
